chunks: Shoot-through in CMOS gates. The question: What is shoot-through on a CMOS logic gate? How can it be prevented?
Shoot-through is when both transistors in a CMOS stage are on at once, so current flows straight from the supply to ground instead of into the load.
It happens briefly on every switching edge. It becomes a real problem when edges are slow, when an input floats, or when two power switches overlap.
Picture a two-door airlock, where the outer door and inner door should never be open together.
While someone swaps doors, there is a moment when both are slightly open and the wind blows straight through. The longer the swap takes, the more wind passes.
Fast switching makes the overlap short.
Current is zero below V tn (NMOS off) and above V DD minus V tp (PMOS off), and peaks at the switching threshold.
The area under this curve, swept by the input edge, is the charge wasted on each transition. A slow edge sweeps it slowly, so more charge is wasted.
Shoot-through (crowbar current): current from supply to ground through both transistors. Switching threshold: the input voltage where the output flips, near half the supply.
Floating input: an input connected to nothing, which can sit at a middle voltage. Schmitt trigger: an input stage that gives a sharp internal edge from a slow signal.
Dead time: a deliberate gap with both switches off.
Use a 5 volts inverter where each transistor needs 1 volts of gate drive to turn on: the NMOS gate 1 volts above ground, the PMOS gate 1 volts below the 5 volts supply.
As the input rises from 0 volts, the NMOS turns on once the input passes 1 volts. The PMOS stays on until the input passes 4 volts.
For input voltages between 1 volts and 4 volts, both are on, and current flows supply to ground. A fast edge crosses this window quickly. A floating input can sit in it all day.
"Shoot-through is when the PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage are on at the same time, so current goes straight from V DD to ground.
It happens during every input transition, between V tn and V DD minus V tp , peaking near mid-rail. It's worst with slow edges or floating inputs.
Prevent it with fast edges, Schmitt-trigger inputs, tied-off unused pins, and in drivers or power stages by giving each FET its own gate signal with break-before-make dead time."
